'''Lilli Hornig''' (née '''Schwenk''', {{langx|cs|Lilli Schwenková}}; March 22, 1921 – November 17, 2017) was a Czech-born American scientist and feminist activist. She worked on the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name=nytimes>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/27/science/donald-hornig-a-bomb-scientist-and-brown-president-dies-at-92.html?_r=0|title=Donald Hornig, Last to See First A-Bomb, Dies at 92|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=November 2, 2014|date=2013-01-26|last1=Martin|first1=Douglas}}</ref><ref name=manhattan>{{cite web|url=https://manhattanprojectvoices.org/oral-histories/lilli-hornigs-interview|title=Voices of the Manhattan Project, Lilli Hornig's Interview|website=Manhattanprojectvoices.org|access-date=November 27, 2017}}</ref>

==Early life==
Hornig was born in [[Ústí nad Labem]] in 1921<ref>{{cite web|url=https://technet.idnes.cz/lilli-hornig-usti-fat-man-nagasaki-dr4-/vojenstvi.aspx?c=A150805_193741_vojenstvi_kuz|title=Destrukce ji nepřekvapila. Rodačka z Ústí pracovala na bombě pro Nagasaki|date=6 August 2015|website=iDNES.cz|access-date=27 November 2017}}</ref> into a [[History of the Jews in the Czech lands|Jewish]] family<ref>{{Cite news |last=Roberts |first=Sam |date=2017-11-21 |title=Lilli Hornig, 96, Dies; A-Bomb Researcher Lobbied for Women in Science |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/21/obituaries/lilli-hornig-96-dies-a-bomb-researcher-lobbied-for-women-in-science.html |access-date=2023-12-23 |issn=0362-4331 |quote=Lilli Schwenk was born into a German-speaking Jewish family on March 22, 1921, in Aussig, in the Sudetenland, which was then part of Czechoslovakia.}}</ref> to Erwin Schwenk, an organic chemist, and the former Rascha Shapiro, a pediatrician.<ref name="obit">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/21/obituaries/lilli-hornig-96-dies-a-bomb-researcher-lobbied-for-women-in-science.html|title=Lilli Hornig, 96, Dies; A-Bomb Researcher Lobbied for Women in Science|first=Sam|last=Roberts|date=21 November 2017|access-date=27 November 2017|website=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

In 1929 her family moved to Berlin. Four years later she and her mother came to the United States, following her father who had moved there to escape the Nazis.<ref name=manhattan/> As her parents were Jewish, her father was threatened with imprisonment in a concentration camp.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://manhattanprojectvoices.org/oral-histories/lilli-hornigs-interview|title=Lilli Hornig's Interview|website=Manhattanprojectvoices.org|access-date=27 November 2017}}</ref>

She obtained her BA from [[Bryn Mawr College|Bryn Mawr]] in 1942 and her Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1950. In 1943, she married [[Donald Hornig]]. They had four children.<ref name="obit" />

==Career==
Hornig accompanied her husband to [[Project Y|Los Alamos]] where he had obtained a job. After she was originally asked to take a typing test, her scientific skills were recognized and she was given a job as a staff scientist working with plutonium chemistry for the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name=chemical>{{cite web|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/hotarticles/cenear/950717/art02.html|title=Chemical & Engineering News|date=July 17, 1995|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=November 2, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Howes2003">{{cite book|author=Ruth H. Howes|title=Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ys0N4rFgt6UC&pg=PA85|date=April 1, 2003|publisher=Temple University Press|isbn=978-1-59213-192-1|pages=85–}}</ref>

When it was later decided that plutonium chemistry was too dangerous for women, Hornig worked in high-explosive lenses instead. While at Los Alamos, she signed a petition urging that the first atom bomb be used on an uninhabited island as a demonstration.<ref name=chemical/>

Hornig later became a chemistry professor at [[Brown University]],<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.brown.edu/articles/2017/12/hornig|title=Lilli Hornig|work=Brown University News|access-date=2018-01-19|language=en}}</ref> and chairwoman of the chemistry department at [[Trinity Washington University|Trinity College]] in Washington, D.C.<ref name=chemical/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.trinitydc.edu/president/2017/12/dr-lilli-hornig-a-prophetic-voice/|title=Dr. Lilli Hornig: A Prophetic Voice {{!}} President's Office - Trinity Washington University|website=www.trinitydc.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2018-01-19|date=2017-12-03|archive-date=2023-02-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213182811/https://www.trinitydc.edu/president/2017/12/dr-lilli-hornig-a-prophetic-voice/|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was appointed by then-current President [[Lyndon Johnson]] as a member of a mission to the Republic of Korea that began the founding of the Korea Institute for Science and Technology.

A feminist, Hornig was the founding director of HERS (Higher Education Resource Services) under the auspices of the Committee for the Concerns of Women in New England Colleges and Universities first organized by Sheila Tobias. She served on equal opportunity committees for the [[National Science Foundation]], the [[National Cancer Institute]], and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. She was the research chair of the Committee for the Equality of Women at Harvard, and consulted with and participated in many studies of women's science education and careers.

Hornig was a Life Trustee of the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]] and was a trustee of the [[Wheeler School]].

==Death==
Hornig died on November 17, 2017, in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], aged 96 from organ failure.<ref name="nyt">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/21/obituaries/lilli-hornig-96-dies-a-bomb-researcher-lobbied-for-women-in-science.html|title=Lilli Hornig, 96, Dies; A-Bomb Researcher Lobbied for Women in Science|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 21, 2017|access-date=November 27, 2017}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
In the 2023 film ''[[Oppenheimer (film)|Oppenheimer]]'', directed by [[Christopher Nolan]], Hornig was portrayed by actor [[Olivia Thirlby]].<ref>{{cite magazine |first1=Molly |last1=Moss |first2=Lewis |last2=Knight |date=July 22, 2023 |title=Oppenheimer cast: Full list of actors in Christopher Nolan film  |magazine=Radio Times |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/oppenheimer-cast-christopher-nolan-murphy/ |access-date=July 24, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Oppenheimer also features a female Czech scientist who worked on the Manhattan Project  |newspaper= The Prague Reporter |date=July 21, 2023 |url=https://www.praguereporter.com/home/2023/7/21/oppenheimer-also-features-a-female-czech-scientist-who-worked-on-the-manhattan-project/ |access-date=4 August 2023}}</ref>
